\chapter{Able, and Willing}
\label{ch:hi-can-and-want}
\hlchaptermodality{70}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what I am able to do, what I want to do, and tell the bare-stem construction apart from the one that keeps the whole -naa form.}

Complete HI-R70-can-want and produce all three unaided: I can come, I want to come, and I cannot come tomorrow.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[saknā]{\hi{सकना} (\emph{saknā}) — to be able to}

\label{lesson:HI-C70-sakna}



\begin{quote}
Two verbs you own: \textbf{\hi{आना}}, to come, and \textbf{\hi{बोलना}}, to speak. You can say that you speak. You cannot say that you \textbf{can} speak, and until you can, a whole examiner's question — \emph{can you come tomorrow?} — has no answer.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{सकना}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{सकना}} — \emph{saknā} — \textbf{to be able to; can, may}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{हिंदी} \hi{बोल} \hi{सकता} \hi{हूँ}.} — \emph{maiṁ hindī bol saktā hūṁ.} — \textbf{I can speak Hindi.}
\end{quote}

Hindi has no separate words for \emph{can}, \emph{could}, \emph{may} and \emph{be able to}. All four run through this one verb, which is why it is worth more than its size.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: \hi{सकना} never stands alone}]
One move does it: \textbf{strip the -\hi{ना} off the first verb and put \hi{सकना} behind it.}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{बोलना}} $\to$ \textbf{\hi{बोल} \hi{सकता} \hi{हूँ}} — I can speak
  \item \textbf{\hi{आना}} $\to$ \textbf{\hi{आ} \hi{सकता} \hi{हूँ}} — I can come
\end{itemize}

The bare stem carries the meaning and \textbf{\hi{सकना}} carries the grammar, so it is \textbf{\hi{सकना}} that takes the ending and sits last, exactly where the verb belongs. \textbf{\hi{सकना}} can never appear on its own: there is no Hindi sentence that is just \emph{maiṁ saktā hūṁ}.

Negate it and you have the most useful excuse in the language: \textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{कल} \hi{नहीं} \hi{आ} \hi{सकता}.} — \emph{I can't come tomorrow.}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bolnā} $\to$ \emph{bol saktā hūṁ}, then \emph{ānā} $\to$ \emph{ā saktā hūṁ}
  \item \emph{maiṁ kal nahīṁ ā saktā}
  \item which of the two verbs takes the ending — \textbf{\hi{सकना}, and it goes last}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What happens to the first verb in front of \textbf{\hi{सकना}}? (\textbf{It drops to its bare stem}.) Can \textbf{\hi{सकना}} be used on its own? (\textbf{No — it always needs another verb in front of it}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%B8\%E0\%A4\%95\%E0\%A4\%A8\%E0\%A4\%BE}{Wiktionary: \hi{सकना}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[chāhnā]{\hi{चाहना} (\emph{chāhnā}) — to want}

\label{lesson:HI-C70-chahna}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{हिंदी} \hi{बोल} \hi{सकता} \hi{हूँ}}. You can now say what you are ABLE to do. The next question an interviewer asks is what you WANT to do.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{चाहना}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{चाहना}} — \emph{chāhnā} — \textbf{to want}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{हिंदी} \hi{बोलना} \hi{चाहता} \hi{हूँ}.} — \emph{maiṁ hindī bolnā chāhtā hūṁ.} — \textbf{I want to speak Hindi.}
\end{quote}

Put it beside the sentence from last lesson and one letter is different, and it is the important one:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{हिंदी} \hi{बोल} \hi{सकता} \hi{हूँ}} — bare stem \textbf{\hi{बोल}}
  \item \textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{हिंदी} \hi{बोलना} \hi{चाहता} \hi{हूँ}} — full infinitive \textbf{\hi{बोलना}}
\end{itemize}

\textbf{\hi{सकना}} takes the stem; \textbf{\hi{चाहना}} takes the whole dictionary form. Both then sit last and take the ending themselves. Getting the two mixed up is the ordinary beginner's error, and hearing them back to back is the cure.

\textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{आना} \hi{चाहता} \hi{हूँ}} — \emph{I want to come}. Say it against \textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{आ} \hi{सकता} \hi{हूँ}} and listen for the \textbf{-\hi{ना}}.

Inside \textbf{\hi{चाहना}} sits the noun \textbf{\hi{चाह}}, \textquotedblleft{}longing,\textquotedblright{} and its cousin \textbf{\hi{चाहिए}} is how Hindi wants a THING rather than an action. They look alike and take opposite kinds of object; this lesson teaches only the verb.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{maiṁ hindī bolnā chāhtā hūṁ}
  \item the pair back to back — \emph{bol saktā hūṁ} / \emph{bolnā chāhtā hūṁ}
  \item \emph{maiṁ ānā chāhtā hūṁ} against \emph{maiṁ ā saktā hūṁ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the two takes the FULL \textbf{-\hi{ना}} form in front of it? (\textbf{\hi{चाहना}}.) Which takes the bare stem? (\textbf{\hi{सकना}}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%9A\%E0\%A4\%BE\%E0\%A4\%B9\%E0\%A4\%A8\%E0\%A4\%BE}{Wiktionary: \hi{चाहना}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[-nā, ek kriyā ke andar]{One verb inside another}

\label{lesson:HI-C70-infinitive-object}



\begin{quote}
Say both sentences from this chapter: \textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{हिंदी} \hi{बोल} \hi{सकता} \hi{हूँ}} and \textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{हिंदी} \hi{बोलना} \hi{चाहता} \hi{हूँ}}. Something is going on in the second one that is worth naming.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the -\hi{ना} form is a noun}]
In \textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{हिंदी} \hi{बोलना} \hi{चाहता} \hi{हूँ}}, the word \textbf{\hi{बोलना}} is not doing verb work. It is sitting where \textbf{\hi{किताब}} sits in \textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{किताब} \hi{देखता} \hi{हूँ}} — in the object slot. The dictionary form of a Hindi verb is also a \textbf{noun}, and it can go anywhere a noun can go:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{किताब} \hi{देखता} \hi{हूँ}.} — \textbf{I look at the book.} — an ordinary noun object
  \item \textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{बोलना} \hi{चाहता} \hi{हूँ}.} — \textbf{I want to speak.} — a VERB in the same slot
\end{itemize}

That is a bigger gift than it looks. You have sixty-nine chapters of verbs, and every single one of their \textbf{-\hi{ना}} forms is now also a thing you can like, want, or talk about.

The order is unchanged, because it never changes: the inner verb comes first as a noun, the outer verb last as the verb. \textbf{\hi{सकना}} is the same construction with one shortcut — it wears the \textbf{-\hi{ना}} away and takes the bare stem — which is why the two lessons before this one belonged together.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{maiṁ kitāb dekhtā hūṁ}
  \item \emph{maiṁ bolnā chāhtā hūṁ}
  \item which word in each sentence is the object — \textbf{kitāb, then bolnā}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What part of speech is \textbf{\hi{बोलना}} in \textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{बोलना} \hi{चाहता} \hi{हूँ}}? (\textbf{A noun, in the object slot}.) What does \textbf{\hi{सकना}} do to that same form? (\textbf{Wears the -\hi{ना} away and takes the bare stem}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[… saknā · … chāhnā]{Can, want, and cannot}

\label{lesson:HI-R70-can-want}



\begin{quote}
One of this chapter's two verbs eats the \textbf{-\hi{ना}} off the verb in front of it and one leaves it alone. Name which is which before you go on.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{maiṁ ā saktā hūṁ} · \emph{maiṁ ānā chāhtā hūṁ}
  \item \emph{maiṁ kal nahīṁ ā saktā}
  \item \emph{maiṁ sochtā hūṁ ki maiṁ ā saktā hūṁ} — a clause inside a clause, with an ability inside that
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the two can never stand without another verb in front of it? (\textbf{\hi{सकना}}.) Which one leaves that verb's \textbf{-\hi{ना}} in place? (\textbf{\hi{चाहना}}.) Then stop.
\end{tcolorbox}
